title: Dynamic arrays
lead: An Essential section on the array that grows and shrinks behind a list, with ODS’s ArrayStack; block copying is Advanced. Arrays are indexed from 0. ArrayStack implements Section 2.1’s List interface and is named by the rule at the end of that passage. Section 1.5 doubled an array only as it grew and wrote m for its capacity; here length(a), a.length in Java, is the capacity, m counts operations, and the array also shrinks when length(a) ≥ 3n.
notes: ODS’s C++ array class, which only its C++ edition describes, and the rest of its chapter on array-based lists, which chapter 3 carries, are left out here.
exercise_notes: No exercise ships with this section yet. OpenDSA’s keyed array-list questions on inserting and deleting at position i and on where the elements sit (ALMCQinsarb, ALMCQdelarb, ALMCQsucc) wait for the converter of OpenDSA’s Khan-format exercises, and its AlistInsertPRO and AlistRemovePRO for the sequence answer type; its questions about a current position (ALMCQinscurr, ALMCQdelcurr, ALTFpred) assume a list model this book does not teach and are left out. Coding Interview University’s “Implement a vector” has no tests of its own and is left out; TheAlgorithms’ dynamic_array.py and ODS’s test_arraystack.py and test_fastarraystack.py are tests with no printed statement. ODS Exercises 2.1 and 2.2 have no published answers and are left out. ODS Exercise 2.7, which needs an ArrayDeque, is held for Section 3.3, and MIT 6.006 Spring 2020 problem 1-3, on a double-ended sequence, is set there.

figures.original_caption: A sequence of add(i,x) and remove(i) operations on an ArrayStack. Arrows denote elements being copied. Operations that result in a call to resize() are marked with an asterisk.

referents.label: i, the index a call names
n, the number of elements stored

footnotes.html: The ${}-1$ in this formula accounts for the special case that occurs when $n=0$ and $\mathrm{length}(a) = 1$.
The bound the proof needs here is $n_i/2-1$, the one its sum above uses and the one it states at the start and at the end. The first case below gives $n_i/2$, but the second gives only $n_i/2-1$.

derivations.what: all calls to resize() take O(m) time
derivations.source: Open Data Structures, 2.1.2 Growing and Shrinking, the proof of Lemma 2.1

assumes.text: Between the $(i-1)$th and the $i$th call to $\mathrm{resize}()$ there are at least $n_i/2-1$ calls to $\mathrm{add}(i,x)$ or $\mathrm{remove}(i)$, where $n_i$ is the value of $n$ during the $i$th call.
There are $m$ calls to $\mathrm{add}(i,x)$ and $\mathrm{remove}(i)$ in all, and $r$ calls to $\mathrm{resize}()$.

then.why: The stretches between consecutive calls to $\mathrm{resize}()$ do not overlap, so their calls add up to at most $m$.

assumes.text: A call to $\mathrm{resize}()$ with $n$ elements stored takes $O(n)$ time.

steps.cap: The $r$ terms $O(n_i)$ share one constant, so their sum is $O$ of the sum of the $n_i$.
A constant factor does not change the class.

derivations.what: at least nᵢ/2 − 1 calls to remove(i) since the last resize
derivations.source: Open Data Structures, 2.1.2 Growing and Shrinking, the proof of Lemma 2.1

assumes.text: After the previous call to $\mathrm{resize}()$, at least $\mathrm{length}(a)/2-1$ elements were stored in $a$.

Each call to $\mathrm{remove}(i)$ takes one element out and each call to $\mathrm{add}(i,x)$ puts one in, so the calls to $\mathrm{remove}(i)$ since the previous resize number at least the elements lost since then.

steps.cap: Since $\mathrm{length}(a)/3 \ge n_i$, putting $n_i$ in its place can only make the right-hand side smaller.
